summary: The what's-new feed now refreshes every 15 minutes instead of every 30
A failed login now shows why it failed instead of "Request failed (401)"
A rejected login no longer reveals whether the username exists
Nodes are listed by hostname again instead of their internal identity UUID
Modpacks now appears in the navbar and in Settings -> Modules once the feature is enabled
Modpacks split into two switches: the subsystem for admins, plus "open authoring to users"
A per-user modpack permission set by hand is now marked as an override and survives the platform switch
The modpack on/off switch no longer exists twice: Settings -> Features owns it, Settings -> Modpacks owns storage
What's new is a modal now, with the latest update on top and the history below it
The what's-new icon stays highlighted while entries exist and only greys out when there is nothing to show
A rejected 2FA setup code is now logged with the reason: clock drift (and by how much) or a code from an older secret
The 2FA wizard explains a rejected code and offers "start over with a new QR"
The disk-quota warning now names the fix (pquota / prjquota) instead of only the problem
Warp: "when the limit is reached" is now settable for multi-connection keys too, not just fixed ones
Warp: inline help for policy, max connections and how external nodes relate to Infrastructure -> Nodes
The sidebar's "New Container" is now a "+" menu that says what you can create and why not
New "My nodes" page: connect your own machine, manage enrollment keys, see its status
Settings -> Users -> Billing shows what a tenant may use and can grant BYON or route-only for N days
The server Reload button is gone; a full Restart is the reliable way to re-read plugins and config
Tickets and Modpacks open their real pages instead of an empty "coming soon" placeholder
The Modpacks module row is re-derived from the feature flags on every start, so it stops showing "Admin" after authoring was opened
Username history moved into Edit Profile, and My Modpacks left the profile menu now that Modpacks has its own navbar entry
The Beam force-update floor now always comes from the signed release manifest; the manual field is gone
The Beam prerelease (dev) update channel was removed; everyone is on the one release stream
DNS now supports 13 providers - Cloudflare, Hetzner, deSEC, IONOS, GoDaddy, Gandi, Bunny, Porkbun, netcup, Namecheap, ClouDNS, OVH and Route 53
Providers that need more than an API token now get the right inputs instead of one box labelled "API Token"
S3 buckets and credentials are defined once under Settings -> Storage Connections; Core Storage, Modpacks and Backups reference one instead of asking again
Settings -> Modpacks can fill in Core's public address from the one you are reached on, instead of you retyping it
Settings -> Nodes now states both ways a machine becomes a node; the old card claimed no manual setup was needed, which stopped being true with the pairing hardening
Settings -> Nodes split: Nodes is the connected list, Node settings holds admission and enroll tokens
Adding a route: subdomain and custom domain are one switch now, so the custom-domain half is findable
My nodes rebuilt: bring-your-own-node and route-only as separate cards, each with its usage against your plan and the deploy stack plus commands
The read-only demo is reachable at /login?demo=1, so a link can drop someone straight into the panel with no account
After connecting a store account the browser is sent back to the panel; needs FRONTEND_URL set, otherwise no link is offered
What's new groups by component: the latest update on top, then everything Core, Panel or Node changed under its own heading instead of in arrival order
Each component is now measured against its OWN installed build, so updating Core while leaving the nodes alone no longer reports the node's changes as installed
The node reports which update-feed position its image was built at, so the panel can tell whether the node specifically is behind
BYON customers can create their own overlay key, so a machine no longer needs an operator to hand one over by e-mail
My machines hands out both secrets at once and fills them into the deploy snippet, instead of leaving a placeholder
Unused overlay keys are listed and revocable - each one counts towards your node limit until it is used or removed
Navbar entries no longer vanish in a narrow window: labels shrink to icons first, then anything left moves into a menu
The server sidebar collapses to a narrow rail, by hand or automatically in a small window; servers stay one click away
In a very narrow window the account and notification buttons collapse behind one menu so the module bar keeps its room

Nodes now notice when a newer Link image is published instead of running whatever the tag pointed at on the day they first started; external and BYON nodes apply it automatically, datacenter nodes wait until no players are connected
Settings -> Nodes -> Node settings now shows which nodes have a pending Link update, with a button to apply it, plus when updates should be applied and how often to check

Fixed non-admin accounts being refused with "Could not verify account restrictions" on every change they tried to make - adding a machine, editing a server, anything - on installs where no demo account had been designated
An external or BYON node now starts its own Link sidecar using a built-in default image, so LINK_IMAGE and NODE_MANAGES_LINK no longer have to be set by hand; nodes inside the cluster are unaffected

Deploy snippets for external, BYON and route-only machines now arrive filled in - node id, enrolment key, Core gRPC and Redis over the overlay - instead of placeholders you had to look up, and no longer carry settings that already match the image defaults
The warp deploy dialog now asks whether the machine is your own external node, a customer's BYON machine or a route-only address, and points at where a customer's entitlement is granted

The RAM chart on a server's overview no longer falls back to the container figure on a quiet server, which sat at the memory limit permanently because Java never gives heap back; the JVM heap reading now survives long gaps between garbage collections
Deleting the last admin is now refused; the delete-user permission can be delegated, so it was possible to remove every admin and leave nobody able to administer the panel
The user list can be sorted by role (admins first, the new default), by name or by newest, and the delete button now stays visible but disabled with the reason instead of quietly disappearing
The list of user accounts moved to Admin -> Users; Settings -> User settings now holds only the rules about how accounts behave, and each page links to the other

Protected addresses moved out of the account dropdown: My machines and Protected addresses now share a tab bar, and Create in the sidebar offers Add a route alongside New server and Add your own machine
A ticket can now say which of your services it is about - a server, one of your own machines, or a protected address - instead of only ever being able to attach a server
The new-ticket form has a What is this about? field listing your servers, machines and protected addresses, and the chosen one shows on the ticket and in the inbox
The custom-tab icon picker now offers 187 searchable icons in a scrollable grid instead of twelve, and hides any icon another tab on the same server already uses
The custom-tab dialog now explains what Direct and Proxied actually do, and warns that a direct URL cannot point at the Dylaris edge because the edge carries Minecraft traffic only

The MOTD editor gained a full toolbar: all sixteen colours and every style including obfuscated, inserted at the cursor, with a per-line character count that ignores the codes because the game does not draw them

My machines and Protected addresses are one page with two tabs instead of two pages: creating a link, deploying it and pointing an address at it now read top to bottom in one place, and Create in the sidebar opens the tab it means
Protected addresses now says so when your account does not include route-only, instead of showing a working-looking form that failed only once you pressed create

The My infrastructure entry in the top bar now appears for anyone who has machines OR protected addresses, admins included; it was limited to non-admins with bring-your-own-node, which left route-only customers and admins with no way in once protected addresses left the account menu

On a platform where bring-your-own-node is off but gateway routing is on, My infrastructure showed only a hardware-is-turned-off notice with protected addresses unreachable behind it; it now opens straight on the half that exists

Console output is no longer thrown away when the log service is briefly unreachable: lines are held and replayed once it is back, and if an outage lasts long enough to overflow the buffer the console says how many lines were lost instead of showing a silent gap
Machines and Minecraft servers now reconnect to the platform on one schedule: twelve tries five seconds apart, then every thirty seconds, starting over again after any successful connection

The deploy snippet for a new machine now names the platform's core service instead of whichever core instance happened to answer, so the address stays right after a redeploy or when core runs more than once
The tunnel subnet in the deploy snippet is filled in from the network core detects around itself when nothing was saved in the warp settings, instead of leaving a placeholder to look up by hand
My infrastructure now has three tabs: your own external machines, bring-your-own-node, and protected addresses. Admins open on their own machines; everyone else lands on the half they came for

Machines that are part of the cluster no longer appear in an admin's list of external and customer machines; the node list can now be asked for one kind at a time and refuses the operator-only kind to anyone else

A machine started with NODE_EXTERNAL now tells the platform so, which is what puts it on the external list and what makes the requires-gateway notice appear; until now no external machine reported it and neither worked
Naming a location is now required when you add a machine: 4 to 20 characters, letters, digits and hyphens. Everything unnamed used to become the same my machine, which made a list of two unreadable

The two keys shown after creating a machine now open beside the form instead of pushing it down the page, and arrive blurred: they are already filled into the compose file below, so the usual path never reads them

An external machine no longer needs the two internal addresses in its compose file: with them left empty it reaches Core and Redis through the tunnel agent, which keeps the current addresses up to date on its own
The deploy snippet for a new machine no longer contains any internal address, so rebuilding the platform network no longer means every owner has to edit and redeploy their file
The tunnel agent is now told where Core and Redis are when it connects and on every check-in, so a machine follows the platform automatically when those addresses move
The deploy snippet for a new machine now carries the certificate pin for the control channel when it is switched on, instead of producing a machine that cannot reach the platform at all
The route-only kit no longer leaves the tunnel agent's status page open on your home network; it is now reachable only from the machine itself

A suspended account now keeps its overlay tunnel for the grace period only (48 hours by default); after that the tunnel is disconnected along with the servers and route credentials, instead of staying up indefinitely

The BYON deploy snippet now carries the Beam LAN fast-path switch, so turning off the TLS listener on port 25523 is a one-word edit in the file the panel gives you instead of something a .env setting silently ignored.
The SFTP brute-force lockout works again: its failed-attempt counter sat outside the node's Redis permissions, so ten wrong passwords in a row never locked anyone out on any node.

Modpack and mod downloads now enforce their size limits instead of quietly cutting a too-large file short and installing it, and a pack manifest can no longer widen those limits by declaring a nonsense file size.

Renaming a file in the desktop client could move it outside its own server directory, including into another server on the same machine; renames are now confined the same way every other file operation already was, and platform-managed files like .node_config.json can no longer be renamed or uploaded over.

A symbolic link placed inside a server directory could be used to read, overwrite or copy files elsewhere on the node; the file browser, the desktop client and SFTP now all refuse a path whose links lead out of the server it belongs to, while links that stay inside keep working.
A single symbolic link anywhere under a server made every backup of that server fail; backups now skip links that lead outside the server and archive contained ones as ordinary files.

An RCON command whose reply kept arriving never finished and was never capped, which could exhaust the node and drop its connection to the panel; replies are now bounded in time and to 64KB, with a note appended when one is cut short.

A domain that was already routed could be claimed a second time, which silently handed the first owner's players to the second one's server; both route-create paths now refuse a domain someone else holds and answer with a conflict instead.

A file transfer in the desktop app was cut off after ten minutes no matter how well it was going, so anything larger than your connection could move in that window failed at the same point every retry and could never be downloaded at all; a transfer is now only abandoned when it actually stops making progress.
Reveal in Explorer now opens the folder holding the downloaded file instead of launching the file in whatever application is registered for it.
The desktop app's "cannot reach the Panel" page printed the connection error without escaping it, so a panel server could place its own markup on the app's privileged page; the error is now escaped.

A single command the node could not process without crashing was retried forever: it took the node down, was re-sent on every restart, and never counted as a failed attempt, so the give-up-and-park path never fired; such a command is now recorded, retried a few times and then parked instead of wedging the node.

While the log service was unreachable, the memory-usage reading was still written for every garbage-collection line and each attempt waited on the network, which could back up far enough to stall the Minecraft server itself; the reading is now sent with the console batches and skipped entirely during an outage.
SFTP on a node that was renamed in the panel listed no servers at all; the folder list was looked up under the node's display name instead of its identity.
A node you own is no longer unpaired automatically after a day offline with no servers on it, so a home machine can be switched off without having to enroll it again.
Removed a leftover node endpoint that accepted no login and let anyone holding a node's id flip that node between online and offline.
Changing a user's role now applies to their current session instead of waiting up to 24 hours: admin rights are read from the account on every request, not from the sign-in token.
An API key now stops working as soon as its creator loses access to the server it points at, instead of keeping the access it was created with.
Password-reset emails are limited to one per minute per address, so nobody can flood an inbox or keep invalidating the reset link you are trying to use.
Live event streams now end when the account behind them is deleted or renamed, instead of continuing on a stale ticket.
A node that reconnects after a brief network drop no longer ends up unreachable from the panel when its old connection finally times out.
Deleting a single sub-server now needs the same delete permission as deleting a whole server.
Creating a node enrollment token is refused once your plan's machine limit is used up, instead of handing out a token that would fail during pairing.
Deleting a library folder can no longer be tricked into wiping the whole library by pointing the path back at the storage root.

Nodes now report backup and restore results on their own private channel, so one machine can no longer close or complete another machine's backups; update Core and every node together, or a node left on the old build will have its backups sit as running until they time out.
Editing a backup target's endpoint, bucket or access key now requires re-entering the secret access key instead of silently reusing the stored one.
A backup target's S3 endpoint is rejected if it carries credentials in the URL, matching the other storage settings forms.
Revoking a node key or a route-only link now also disconnects the machine from the private network, instead of only blocking it from joining again.
The per-account route limit now also applies to routes created for managed servers, not just route-only links, so disabling route creation for an account actually stops it everywhere.
A warp region with machines still connected can no longer be deleted, which used to leave those tunnels up with no way to remove them.

Beam file transfer now requires the SFTP capability on a server. Members with only read access to files could previously write, delete and rename anything through Beam; grant them the SFTP permission if they should keep that access.
The limits on proxied tabs per server and share links per user are now applied when a tab is edited or a share link is re-rolled, not only when a tab is created.
The file manager download limit from the settings page is now actually enforced; it had no effect before, so raise it if your users download world folders larger than the configured value.

Changing the endpoint, bucket or access key of the modpack storage or of a shared storage connection now requires re-entering the secret key, so a saved credential can no longer be pointed at a different host by someone who cannot read it.

Saving a modpack's Solder settings without sending the visibility field no longer makes a private pack public, and renaming a modpack no longer wipes its Solder slug and takes it off the public pack list.

The Beam download link and release manifest are now fetched through a guard that refuses internal addresses, and the link itself must be a plain http/https URL, so the setting can no longer be used to read internal endpoints through the public download route.
The billing payment URL is now validated as an http/https address before it is saved, because it is rendered as the link on every tenant's payment banner.

The SMTP password is now encrypted in the database like the other stored credentials. An existing one stays in plain text until you open Settings and save the mail form once with the password re-entered.
The stored password hash can no longer appear in an API response by accident; it is now excluded from user data at the type level instead of being cleared by hand at each endpoint.
Backups and restores were being dropped by the node without ever starting, leaving the run stuck at queued. They run again.
A node started without a Beam ticket secret no longer opens its LAN fast-path listener with a certificate anyone could reproduce; it now refuses to start that listener and says so in the log.
Installing a server from a ZIP or a modpack can no longer be steered into another server's directory by a symlink left in the target folder.

When moving a server between nodes, the receiving node now only probes private LAN addresses the source could genuinely own, and stops after the first few, so a move cannot be pointed at an unrelated host or made to stall.
A node can no longer pick up a new identity from a background reconnect. Re-pairing now only happens at startup, where it still asks for a recovery token first.

A node no longer looks up its public address on every heartbeat, and a failed lookup keeps the last known address instead of replacing it with an internal one that would then be shown as the node's address.

Resetting a node's pairing now actually recovers it. A node that still held its old credentials on disk ignored the recovery token and could not reconnect at all; it now presents the token alongside whatever it has cached.

After a pairing reset the console of every already-running server stayed silent, because those servers kept the previous Redis credentials. The node now notices that and restarts them so console output and commands come back.
A server held down for exceeding its disk limit can no longer be brought back up by the recovery pass that rebuilds missing containers.
A restore now extracts into a directory with an unpredictable name, so nothing running inside a server's own container can redirect the restore by placing a link where it was about to write.
A restore that is killed part-way no longer leaves its half-extracted copy of the world behind forever, taking up the server's own disk allowance.
Deleting a server always frees its port again, including when its container had already been removed. Those ports used to stay reserved for good and slowly used up the range.

Downloading a node-local backup now only ever returns a real archive. A link placed in the backup folder from inside a server's own container used to be followed, and its target streamed out as if it were a backup.
A backup run refuses to write through a link left in the backup folder instead of creating its archive, and the panel no longer lists such a link as a downloadable backup.
A proxied custom tab is now checked on the node side too: only a plain request path is accepted, so nothing can steer the request away from the server's own container.
Installing or removing a mod, and the automatic EULA accept during setup, now stay inside the server's own folder even if a link was left in the mods or plugins directory.
Stopping a server now always shuts the Minecraft process down cleanly and lets it save, instead of it being killed together with the container on some stop paths.
A single very long or unusual console line no longer freezes the console, which previously also stalled the server itself.
A file-transfer ticket can no longer be presented to the panel API as a login session; only tokens issued for the panel itself are accepted.

A server move now refuses a transfer that sends more data than the source announced, so a misbehaving source cannot fill the target machine's disk, and it will not write through a link left in the target folder.
A download from a server that stops responding now fails with an error instead of appearing to hang forever, while large transfers stay uncapped.

Updated the gRPC and database libraries: a client could previously flood the node connection with rapidly aborted requests and drive the server's CPU up, and the Postgres driver carried a memory-safety bug.
Updated the gRPC library so the beam file-transfer server can no longer be driven to high CPU by a client that opens and aborts requests in a rapid loop.
A node on your own machine again avoids picking a local Docker subnet that would shadow the tunnel, after the tunnel interface was renamed.

The node IP allowlist is now checked when a machine joins the tunnel, where its real address is visible. It previously ran where every customer machine looked like the same internal address, so it could not tell them apart.
A node can now only read the SFTP passwords of users who actually have a server on it, instead of every account on the platform.
A node can no longer write another server's migration state or a peer's transfer address.
Beam's fast local file transfer now works on your own machine. It needed a platform-wide secret that your machine never receives, so it silently stayed off.
The route-only deploy snippet has a Windows (Docker Desktop) variant that points at the right address for a Minecraft server running on Windows.
Turning on two-factor authentication now asks for your password. Without it, anyone who got hold of a logged-in session could attach their own authenticator to your account and lock you out.
The Beam download is checked against the signed release before it reaches you, even when an operator points it at their own mirror. That check used to be skipped entirely for a mirror.

Each Minecraft server now gets its own database credential instead of sharing one per machine, so one server can no longer reach another's console. Restart your servers once so they pick up the new credential.

You can point your own domain at the platform after proving you control it: add the CNAME or A record within four hours and it verifies itself. A domain you fail to set up twice is blocked for your account only, and a TXT record unblocks it without a support ticket.
Beam file transfer now works on a node you run yourself. Your machine never receives the platform-wide key, so it rejected every transfer; tickets now carry a proof it can check with its own key.
Beam transfers through the relay work again. The relay connection was refused on every node because the agent was not allowed to read the certificate it had to check.

Asking for the Beam app on a platform we do not build for now says so plainly, instead of showing you an internal note about release manifests. A download that fails because the release feed is unreachable now says that instead, so the two are no longer confusable.

Bringing your own domain now tells you the real record to create, and accepts it once you have. The instruction named only the first part of the target, and the check looked for that same incomplete value, so a correctly pointed domain could never verify by CNAME.

Adding a route on your own domain now tells you the record to create and that you have four hours to do it. Until now the route was accepted in silence and simply disappeared when the deadline passed.
Opening the server wizard without a node now offers a way to add one. It explained that a node was needed and then gave you nothing but a Close button.

Turning on gRPC TLS with a value like 1 or True now works on nodes too. Core accepted those spellings and nodes only accepted the exact word true, so the setting could switch on at one end and leave every node unable to reach Core.

The control channel between Core and your nodes is now encrypted by default. Nodes running inside the cluster switch over on their own. A bring-your-own node needs a fresh deploy snippet from the panel first, because it has to be told which certificate to trust - an older snippet will not start until you replace it.

Edge errors appear on the gateway errors page again. The service was renamed from gate to edge and the page kept looking for the old name, so it always showed nothing for the component that carries all player traffic.

The admin Status page now says WHY a node is offline instead of only that it is, and flags scoped Redis credentials that should exist but do not. A missing one silences that server's console while everything else still looks healthy.
Long explanations on the Status page are no longer cut off mid-sentence. The reason a node cannot connect is exactly the part that used to be truncated away.

The Status page now checks the storefront connection. A wrong shared key or an unreachable store used to look exactly like a customer who simply had not connected their account, so a broken billing link was invisible.

API keys now reach more than RCON. A key can read a server, start and stop it, send console commands and read the log back, read stats, list and trigger backups, and read the account's metered usage - each one only if the key was minted with that permission and scoped to that server.

The API Keys page now offers every permission a key can carry instead of just RCON exec, and it lists them by category. It reads the permission catalogue directly, so a permission added later shows up on its own.

Admins decide whether users other than admins may hold API keys at all, and which permissions those keys may carry. Both are under Settings, Features. The switch is OFF on a fresh install, and turning it off stops keys that already exist rather than only blocking new ones.

The BYON toggle is now disabled while game traffic runs on IP:Port. A tenant node forces gateway routing on its own side, so with no gateway there was nothing for it to join and the switch only produced an enrolment screen for machines that could never connect.
The billing banner no longer polls in the background on installs with no storefront connected.
Creating a user from the admin panel works again. The password field was silently dropped on the way in, so every attempt failed with "Password is required" no matter what was typed.

Reading a server console over the API no longer comes back empty when the request does not name a sub-server. It now follows whichever sub-server is running, which is the one commands were already being sent to.

Naming a sub-server now refuses characters it cannot use instead of quietly dropping them. Before, a name with a space, a slash or an accent was silently turned into a different one, and a name over 50 characters produced a sub-server that could never be switched to.
Switching to a sub-server that does not exist is refused instead of accepted. It used to be recorded as the active one, which left the panel pointing at nothing while the old sub-server kept running.

Disk usage is reported per sub-server again on storage that cannot hold a filesystem quota, which is most self-hosted setups. The Overview breakdown was empty there, and the maximum-sub-servers setting had nothing to count.

SFTP now honours what a member was actually granted. Anyone invited to a server could open a full read-write SFTP session on it no matter which permissions were set, including none - they could read server.properties with its RCON password, replace files and delete the server jar, while the same account was refused every one of those actions in the panel.
Granting someone access to a whole account now gives them SFTP to that account's servers. It only ever worked for access granted server by server.

The live event stream no longer tells an account about servers it cannot see. Change notifications naming a server were broadcast to every signed-in session, which disclosed other people's server IDs and when they were active.

A scheduled chat message to a server that is not running is now reported as failed instead of being stored up. Those messages used to queue without limit while the server was down and then all arrive at once on the next start, part of them while it was still booting.

Installing a mod with a path in its file name is refused instead of accepted. Such a request was answered with success, the file was written under a different name than the one recorded, and removing it from the panel then missed.
A mod download that is redirected to another host is refused. Downloads are pinned to the Modrinth CDN when the install is requested, and that pin previously only covered the first hop.

A server stopped for hitting its storage limit no longer shows as online afterwards. The stats collector overwrote the hold a few seconds after it was set, which also stopped the panel from refusing to start the server again.

Giving someone access to a server, changing what they may do, or taking it away is now written to that server's audit log. Those entries only ever appeared for an older invite screen the panel no longer uses, so access granted through Access left no trace at all. Account-wide access is recorded in the platform audit log.
A shared custom tab is now served only on the dedicated tab-proxy origin; the panel origin answers whether the link works and nothing more.
Opening a private tab share link now needs the same permission as seeing that tab in the panel, instead of merely being able to see the server.

A custom tab's share link can now be given an expiry date. Until now the field existed everywhere except where it was set, so no link could ever expire; rotating a link that has run out gives you a working one again.
The custom tabs screen now shows when a share link expires, marks one that already has, and says so when share links cannot work yet because the server has no separate tab-proxy origin.

RCON now follows the sub-server you switch to. The setting is stored once per server but lives in each sub-server's server.properties, so after a switch the panel unlocked the player tools while nothing was listening; it is now written before the server restarts.

A support ticket can now only be filed about a server you can actually open. Any account could name any server id, and the reply came back carrying that server's name - and the ticket then put that server in the assigned supporter's list.

Player management is now its own permission. Letting someone ban, kick, op or whitelist used to require handing them every RCON command the server has plus read access to the whole filesystem; the View players and Manage players permissions now cover exactly that job and nothing else.
The Players tab now appears for anyone with the View players permission instead of keying on the right to start the server.

A backup schedule the system cannot read is now refused instead of saved. Values like "daily" or "every 6H" were accepted, listed as a scheduled job, and never ran once - which you would only discover the day you needed the backup.

Editing one setting on a backup job no longer wipes the others. Changing only the schedule through the API cleared the job's name, its sub-server, its file patterns and its storage, and switched the job off - so adjusting how often a backup ran stopped it running at all.

Changing an account's password now signs out every other session it had. Until now a reset stopped the old password working but left any session already open alive for up to a day - including the one you reset the password to get rid of. The person doing the change stays signed in.

An outstanding password-reset link now stops working the moment the password is changed by any other route. Someone who received a reset mail they did not request and reacted by changing their password themselves was leaving that link live, and it could still take the account over.

Turning on "require security questions during password reset" now shows how many accounts it does not cover. Accounts with no questions stored skip the step by design, and until now nothing said that this is every account that existed before the switch was flipped.

Usernames are now reserved without regard to capitalisation, so a name like "NewComer" can no longer be taken next to an existing "newcomer". Existing accounts are untouched; if two such names already exist, the startup log names them and the rest of the protection still applies.

A store purchase now applies the node count the customer paid for. Until now the store only told the panel "this account is paid" and never how much it bought, so a customer who paid for five nodes stayed on the default plan's limit until an admin raised it by hand. The purchased count arrives as a per-user override and follows upgrades, dunning and cancellation.

The modpack delivery check now downloads a real pack file to decide whether your public mirror is readable, instead of only asking the mirror's base address. An object-storage endpoint that refuses anonymous requests with an unusual error was being reported as publicly reachable, so "public" delivery looked available when players could not have downloaded anything.

Pages for switched-off features now say so instead of looking ready to use. The Solder key and client pages showed an empty list and a live create button on a platform with modpacks turned off, the Modrinth page offered to connect a token that could not be saved, and the billing settings showed built-in defaults as if they were your stored values.

"My infrastructure" no longer opens the protected-addresses half on a platform where bring-your-own-node is switched off. Everything under it was being refused, including for admins, so the tab could only ever look broken.

Protected addresses are now part of what you buy. Every BYON node and every route-only location brings a number of addresses with it, and they all go into one shared pool, so it does not matter which location spends them. Add-on packs top the same pool up.

If your account holds more than your subscription covers, you now get an email and a warning banner with a 3 day deadline. Miss it and everything on the account is disconnected, not just the excess, because we do not choose which of your machines to stop. Nothing is deleted and it all comes back once you are within your limits.
A red banner now appears when your account is over its limit, naming the exact deadline after which everything stops. It takes priority over the payment banner because it is the nearer deadline.

Billing checks now run once immediately when the server starts instead of waiting for the next hourly pass. A grace period that ran out while the server was down used to go unnoticed for up to an hour after it came back.

With per-owner network isolation switched on, gateway-routed servers were unreachable for players: the tunnel sidecar was not on the isolated networks and could not resolve the server it was pointed at. It now joins every one of them, on a reserved address so it cannot take one a server is holding.
Your address allowance now only counts subdomains on our own domains. A domain you own and point at the edge with a CNAME no longer uses one up, so you can add as many of your own as you like.

A banner now warns you at 80% of the traffic your subscription covers, and tells you whether reaching the limit will bill you or stop your services. Which one it is depends on whether you have switched metered billing on.
DNS settings have moved out of the panel and into the gateway hub's own admin page; re-enter the provider credential there, and remove any DNS_ variables from Core

Settings -> Gateway now has an Automatic DNS card: pick your DNS provider, paste its API token and name the zones it may write into, and the gateway keeps the edge and beam records pointed at whatever is online. The token is stored by the gateway, not by this platform.

Settings -> Gateway now also holds the certificate settings: a contact address, the certificate authority and the switch that makes the gateway obtain and renew the beam relay's TLS certificate. It shows per name whether one was issued, when it expires and the last error, which is the only place that error is visible.
Saving the Beam settings no longer pins whichever relay was discovered as a permanent manual override, which used to end relay failover silently.
The Beam settings page now shows the relay in use separately from the optional override, and explains what the throttles, upload limits and hardware reference actually do.
The DNS check now also checks the API hostname and the Beam relay hostname, and dials both.
Outgoing email can now be sent through Resend instead of an SMTP server; pick the provider under Settings, User settings, Email.
User settings is now five tabs instead of seven cards stacked down one page, and everything on it saves through the same bar at the bottom.
Changing a sign-in rule and later an auto-delete rule no longer silently reverts the first: both edit one shared copy of the account policy now.
The Gateway and Nodes settings pages now use a tab bar instead of a second sidebar next to the settings sidebar.
A storage connection can now be tested from inside the dialog, before it is saved, and the dialog has a help panel with the right values for Cloudflare R2, Hetzner and AWS.
Modpack storage no longer starts on a preselected provider that was not actually configured; creating a modpack is blocked with a pointer to the setting until storage is chosen.
The DNS settings can now test the provider token and list the zones it can see, and zones are switched on and off individually instead of typed as one comma-separated line.

A Warp key set to Fixed no longer stores a connection limit it does not use, and the help text no longer promises a pinned overlay address the form never sent or an eviction by idleness it does not do.
The Gateway settings tab formerly called Hub Admin is now Hub Redis access, which is what it actually issues.
Settings has a search box: type what a setting does, not which page it is on, and it takes you straight to the right page and tab.
Everything in the panel now saves the same way: one Save and Discard bar at the bottom, which also warns before you navigate away with unsaved changes.
Server properties no longer writes the file on every keystroke in simple mode; edits are marked and saved together.
Toggling a navigation module, changing its audience or reordering it now confirms it worked instead of succeeding silently.
Maintenance mode, ticket settings and billing defaults no longer discard your edits without a word when you leave the page.
Checkboxes and switches are styled to match the panel and have proper hover, focus and disabled states; the cursor no longer changes halfway across a checkbox row.
The server display, proxy config and RCON pages now use the same save bar as everything else, and warn before you leave with unsaved edits.
Settings that are easy to misread now carry a help button that explains what the value actually does, starting with routing mode, file access, storage backend and API-key capabilities.
The fleet placement defaults and the Link update policy now warn before you leave with unsaved changes instead of dropping them.
Switching tabs inside a settings page with unsaved changes now asks what to do instead of discarding them.
A save that fails or that you cancel no longer navigates away afterwards, which used to discard the very edits the prompt was protecting.
Billing defaults stayed marked as unsaved forever after a successful save; the bar and the navigation prompt would not go away.
A stalled save no longer leaves you unable to save or discard, and toast messages are now announced to screen readers.
Searching the settings while you have unsaved changes now asks first instead of navigating away.
Saving the email settings without naming a provider no longer silently switches a Resend setup back to SMTP.
The feature-flag endpoint no longer resolves modpack storage on every request, which could make login wait on the shared storage limiter.
Bringing your own node or a protected address now requires an active subscription. Accounts that had bought nothing were previously treated as having no limit at all.
When infrastructure is locked, the panel now says whether you still need to connect your store account or whether you need a plan, and links straight to the right place.
A new SETUP environment variable keeps the first-run setup page closed once an administrator exists. Set SETUP=true together with ADMIN_SECRET and restart if you ever need to create another admin.
Plan tiers are gone from the settings. A tenant's limits are now set directly on their account, which is what the store has always written.
The Hub Redis access tab was removed from the gateway settings.
The player head beside your username in the navbar shows up again when a Minecraft username is set.
The setup page now explains itself and offers a way back when you reach it on an instance that is already set up.
Save and Discard moved out of the bar at the bottom of the screen and into the corner of each settings box, so the button that writes a setting sits next to the setting.
Settings pages that wrote one thing through several boxes are now one box with sections, which is Modpacks, Beam, Features, Gateway and DDoS protection.
A dialog with a help panel now stays centred whether the help is open or closed, instead of sitting left of centre and jumping when it opens.
Every settings page now uses the same heading, the same box and the same save control, so the six different header styles and five ways of saving are gone.

Modpack builds can now be checked against newer Minecraft versions: every version line shows whether the client-only, server-only and both-sided mods are all available, and a version that is not fully green expands to the mods that would be lost, each with its Modrinth link.
A modpack build can be moved to another Minecraft version. The move always creates a NEW build with every mod resolved to its version for the target, so the build it came from stays exactly as it is.

A modded server has a new Minecraft version tab with the same availability check as modpacks, and can be moved to another Minecraft version with its mods carried across. Mods with no version for the target are listed first and are only removed if you say so.

A server version change now runs as one step on the node: it stops, swaps the mod jars, reinstalls the server software at the new version and starts again. The world and the configuration are untouched.

A server can be copied to a second sub-server before a version change, so the old version stays one switch away. The server has to be stopped first, because a running server's world files would be copied while they are being written.

Jars placed on a server by hand over SFTP or the file manager are now listed, and can be identified against Modrinth by their file hash. Once identified they take part in version checks and are carried across a version change like any other mod.
Creating a modpack now says up front that only content linked to Modrinth can be version-checked, so hand-uploaded files are a known limitation rather than a surprise at migration time.

Modrinth responses over 512 KB are no longer cached. One version list can weigh over a megabyte, and the cache keeps one entry per filter combination for an hour, so the large end of that was the only thing here growing with use rather than with fleet size.

Settings, Modpacks now has a Mod metadata cache card. It stays on the Redis the panel already runs on unless you point it somewhere else, which nothing requires you to do; it is there for operators who would rather their control plane never shared memory with a cache.
The bundled Redis now runs with a memory ceiling and evicts cached entries first. Without one it would refuse writes when full, and one of those writes is queueing a command to a node.

Mod changelogs are no longer kept in the metadata cache. They were about two thirds of a typical Modrinth version list and nothing in the panel ever showed them; every published build stays listed, since installing an older one is what the version picker is for.
Ending a subscription entirely now starts the same 72-hour countdown a downgrade does; before, cancelling everything left everything running.
Administrators no longer need a subscription of their own to add a node or a protected address on their own platform.
A separate cache Redis that is unreachable at startup no longer silently falls back to the panel Redis, and the settings page now says it is not answering instead of showing a healthy tick.
Moving a server to another Minecraft version now downloads every mod before removing anything, so a failed download leaves the server untouched instead of starting it without that mod.
The cross-version mod check reported some mods as unavailable on every version after the first once part of the answer was already cached; it now checks every mod on every version.
A Minecraft version move the node could not carry out now puts the server's recorded version and mod list back, instead of leaving them describing a move that never happened.
Copying a sub-server onto a name that already exists is refused instead of merging the copy's mod list into the existing one.
Migrating a modpack build now says which mods could not be added to the new build, instead of reporting a plain success.
Identifying unknown jars no longer follows a symlink out of the server directory, which could reveal the size and checksums of files elsewhere on the node.
Identifying a jar that is a second copy of a mod you already have is now refused and explained, instead of quietly pointing the existing mod at the stray file.
When Modrinth cannot be reached, identifying jars now says so instead of reporting that the files are not on Modrinth.
Identifying more than 200 unknown jars at once now works; it used to be refused outright, which is the case an imported server hits first.
The panel no longer sends its signed request, or the DNS credential with it, to whatever answers when the gateway hub name has not resolved yet.
Clicking Settings in the top bar, or a server in the sidebar, while editing a form on that page no longer discards the edits without asking.

A connected bring-your-own-node machine counted twice against the node limit. Customers were refused a second machine, shown the wrong usage, and could be warned and cut off while exactly within their plan.

The Link update policy and check interval chosen in Settings survive a Redis restart. Until now they were only mirrored when saved, so a node starting afterwards fell back to updating its own Link on its own while the panel still showed the setting the operator had picked.

Proxied custom tabs are now served on their own hostname instead of a path under the panel, which is what finally makes BlueMap and Dynmap work in a tab. Set TAB_PROXY_HOST_SUFFIX on Core and point a wildcard DNS record and certificate at it; until you do, proxied tabs and their share links stay switched off. Direct tabs are unaffected.

A new Custom Tabs entry in the navigation shows every proxied tab you can reach, grouped by server, using the full width of the window instead of the strip beside the server menu. Enable it under Settings, Modules.

The limit on proxied custom tabs is now counted per user instead of per server, with a second limit across all of a user's servers. Defaults are 3 per server and 10 in total, both adjustable under Settings, Features. Previously one person could spend the whole allowance of a server they shared with others.

A proxied custom tab can be tied to one sub-server. It points at a port inside the container and the container runs whichever sub-server is started, so an unpinned tab follows whatever is running while a pinned one stays hidden until its own world is up, instead of quietly showing a different one.
You can pick your own share link for a custom tab instead of the generated one, for example /c/max-survival-map. Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, and it has to still be free.

Proxied custom tabs could not authorize at all: the browser blocked the panel's call to the tab's own host because the security policy did not list it. Every proxied tab showed an authorization error.
A copied share link now points at the share host instead of the panel's own address, so handing one out no longer discloses where your panel lives.

Pinning a custom tab to one sub-server had no effect: the tab was served no matter which sub-server was running, so a map tab could show a different world than the one it was named after. The pin is now enforced and a mismatch says so instead.
A custom tab pinned to a sub-server is now hidden from the server tab bar and the Custom Tabs page while a different sub-server is running, instead of appearing and then refusing to load.
When a proxied custom tab cannot be authorized because the browser refused the call, the panel now names the tab host and the setting to check instead of reporting a generic connection failure.

A restore that was killed part-way through could leave its staging directory behind for good, a full copy of the world counting against the server's disk limit. It happened only when the random name came out short, so the cleanup that was meant to remove it did not recognise it.

An upload through the desktop app that was cut off mid-transfer left its partial file behind for good when it went into a nested folder such as a plugin's config directory. The cleanup only looked in the top two levels of a server.
A player could set the memory figure on your server's live chart by typing a fake garbage-collector line into chat. Only the JVM's own output is read for it now.
Rebuilt on Go 1.26.7. The previous toolchain carried eight standard-library flaws that Core's own code reaches, including two in the HTTP server and one in the template engine.
Rebuilt on Go 1.26.7, closing seven standard-library flaws the node reaches.
Rebuilt on Go 1.26.7, closing two standard-library flaws the log shipper reaches.

Creating an API key and setting your security questions now ask for your password again, plus a two-factor code if you use one. Both grant access that outlives your current sign-in, so a session someone else got hold of can no longer turn itself into permanent access.
The API key dialog and the security questions form now ask for your password before saving, and for an authenticator code if two-factor is on.
A database hiccup while refreshing one node's SFTP access list no longer deletes the published credentials for every user on that node, which logged them out of SFTP until the next sync.

Modpack exports can no longer carry a file path that escapes the instance folder: the .mrpack manifest, the Solder zips and the stored target paths are all checked now, not just the server-pack and Solder renders.

A launcher that presents a Solder API key or a client id now still sees the public modpack list: a credential adds the packs it unlocks instead of replacing the catalogue, and a key no longer suppresses a client whitelist.

Aligning a mod to a Modrinth version now downloads only from the Modrinth CDN and no longer puts the version number straight into a storage path, so a crafted Modrinth version cannot steer where the file is fetched from or written to.
Updating or editing a mod that two modpack builds share no longer changes or deletes the file the other build uses, which previously made that build fail to render.
